\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Background}
Iwasawa theory attaches to an arithmetic object --- classically an ideal class
group, and for us the arithmetic of an elliptic curve $E/\mathbb{Q}$ --- a module
over the \emph{Iwasawa algebra}
\[
\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}_p[[T]],
\]
the ring of formal power series in one variable $T$ with coefficients in the ring
$\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers. Up to pseudo-isomorphism, finitely generated
torsion $\Lambda$-modules are classified by a \emph{characteristic element}, a
nonzero $f \in \Lambda$. Two integer invariants of $f$ control the coarse
structure of the module: the \emph{$\mu$-invariant} and the
\emph{$\lambda$-invariant}. Writing $f = \sum_{i\ge 0} a_i T^i$ with $a_i \in
\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $v_p$ the $p$-adic valuation,
\[
\mu_p(f) = \min_i v_p(a_i), \qquad
\lambda_p(f) = \min\{\, i : v_p(a_i) = \mu_p(f)\,\}.
\]
The Weierstrass preparation theorem gives the equivalent factorization
$f = p^{\mu}\cdot U \cdot P$ with $U \in \Lambda^{\times}$ a unit and $P$ a
distinguished polynomial of degree exactly $\lambda$.

\subsection{The supersingular setting and Matsuno's formula}
When $E$ has \emph{supersingular} reduction at $p$, one works with Pollack's $\pm$
$p$-adic $L$-functions and Sprung's sharp/flat ($\sharp/\flat$) decomposition, each
component carrying its own invariants. Matsuno's formula compares
$\lambda$-invariants under a quadratic twist by a square-free integer $D$, and a
natural refinement predicts that the sharp/flat $\lambda$-difference should carry a
term proportional to the $\mu$-invariant precisely when $\mu \neq 0$.

\subsection{Contribution}
We isolate and prove the algebraic core underlying this bookkeeping. Modelling
characteristic elements by polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$, we prove: (1) an
\emph{additivity bridge}, that both $\mu$ and $\lambda$ are additive under
multiplication, by two arguments from two different areas of mathematics; and
(2) a \emph{twist formula}, that for the modelled twist factor
$\mathrm{twist}_{c,k} = p^k X^{ck}$ the $\lambda$-shift equals $c\cdot\mu$ of the
twist and is nonzero exactly when $\mu\neq0$ and $c\neq0$.

\section{Definitions and the algebraic model}
We replace the power-series variable $T$ by a polynomial variable $X$ and work in
$\mathbb{Z}[X]$. Throughout, $p$ is a fixed prime.

\begin{definition}[Reduction]
For $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ we write $\overline{f} \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ for the
reduction of $f$ modulo $p$, obtained by applying $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{F}_p$ to
each coefficient. Reduction is a ring homomorphism, so
$\overline{a\cdot b} = \overline{a}\cdot\overline{b}$.
\end{definition}

Every nonzero $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ has a \emph{content} $\cont(f)$, the
normalized nonnegative gcd of its coefficients, and a \emph{primitive part}
$\pp(f)$, with $f = \cont(f)\cdot\pp(f)$ and $\pp(f)$ primitive. Gauss's Lemma
gives multiplicativity of both: $\cont(fg) = \cont(f)\cont(g)$ and
$\pp(fg) = \pp(f)\pp(g)$.

\begin{definition}[$\mu$-invariant]
For nonzero $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, $\mu_p(f) = v_p\big(\cont(f)\big)$.
Equivalently $\mu_p(f) = \min_i v_p(a_i)$ for $f = \sum a_i X^i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\lambda$-invariant]
For nonzero $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, $\lambda_p(f) =
\trdeg\big(\overline{\pp(f)}\big)$, the trailing degree of the mod-$p$ reduction
of the primitive part. Equivalently, $\lambda_p(f)$ is the first index $i$ at
which $v_p(a_i)$ attains its minimum $\mu_p(f)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Reduction of a primitive polynomial is nonzero]\label{lem:nonzero}
For every nonzero $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, $\overline{\pp(f)} \neq 0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $\overline{\pp(f)} = 0$, then $p$ divides every coefficient of $\pp(f)$, i.e.
the constant $p$ divides $\pp(f)$. Primitivity forces $p$ to be a unit in
$\mathbb{Z}$, contradicting $p \ge 2$.
\end{proof}

\section{The additivity bridge}

\begin{theorem}[$\mu$ is additive]\label{thm:mu}
For nonzero $f, g \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, $\mu_p(fg) = \mu_p(f) + \mu_p(g)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Gauss's Lemma $\cont(fg) = \cont(f)\cont(g)$, with both contents nonzero. The
$p$-adic valuation is additive on nonzero integers, so
$\mu_p(fg) = v_p(\cont(f)\cont(g)) = v_p(\cont(f)) + v_p(\cont(g)) = \mu_p(f) +
\mu_p(g)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\lambda$ is additive]\label{thm:lambda}
For nonzero $f, g \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, $\lambda_p(fg) = \lambda_p(f) + \lambda_p(g)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By multiplicativity of the primitive part and the fact that reduction is a ring
homomorphism, $\overline{\pp(fg)} = \overline{\pp(f)}\cdot\overline{\pp(g)}$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero} both factors are nonzero in $\mathbb{F}_p[X]$. Since
$\mathbb{F}_p[X]$ is an integral domain, the trailing degree is additive under
multiplication of nonzero elements (the lowest-degree terms multiply without
cancellation). Hence $\lambda_p(fg) = \trdeg(\overline{\pp(f)}) +
\trdeg(\overline{\pp(g)}) = \lambda_p(f) + \lambda_p(g)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorems~\ref{thm:mu} and \ref{thm:lambda} together are the mechanism by which
factorizations of characteristic elements translate into additive relations
between Iwasawa invariants: for $f = f_1\cdots f_r$ one gets
$\mu_p(f) = \sum_j \mu_p(f_j)$ and $\lambda_p(f) = \sum_j \lambda_p(f_j)$.
\end{remark}

\section{The Matsuno-type twist formula}

\begin{lemma}[Constant $p^k$]\label{lem:pk}
For $k\ge0$, $\mu_p(p^k) = k$ and $\lambda_p(p^k) = 0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The content of the constant $p^k$ is $p^k$, so $\mu_p(p^k) = v_p(p^k) = k$; its
primitive part is $1$, of trailing degree $0$, so $\lambda_p(p^k) = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Power $X^n$]\label{lem:xn}
For $n\ge0$, $\mu_p(X^n) = 0$ and $\lambda_p(X^n) = n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The content of $X^n$ is $1$, so $\mu_p(X^n) = 0$; $X^n$ is monic hence primitive,
and its reduction $X^n \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ has trailing degree $n$, so
$\lambda_p(X^n) = n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Twist factor]
For nonnegative integers $c$ and $k$, set $\mathrm{twist}_{c,k} = p^{k} X^{c k}
\in \mathbb{Z}[X]$. It is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Invariants of the twist factor]\label{prop:twist}
$\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = k$ and $\lambda_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = ck$; in
particular $\lambda_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = c\cdot\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k})$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorems~\ref{thm:mu}, \ref{thm:lambda} to $p^k \cdot X^{ck}$ with
Lemmas~\ref{lem:pk}, \ref{lem:xn}: $\mu_p = k+0 = k$ and $\lambda_p = 0+ck = ck =
c\cdot k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Matsuno-type twist formula]\label{thm:matsuno}
Let $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ be nonzero. For all $c,k\ge0$,
\[
\lambda_p\big(f\cdot\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}\big)
= \lambda_p(f) + c\cdot\mu_p\big(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}\big).
\]
The correction term $c\cdot\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = ck$ is literally
proportional to the $\mu$-invariant of the twist.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lambda}, $\lambda_p(f\cdot\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = \lambda_p(f)
+ \lambda_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k})$; by Proposition~\ref{prop:twist},
$\lambda_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = ck = c\cdot\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k})$.
\end{proof}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:mu} the twist also shifts $\mu$ additively:
$\mu_p(f\cdot\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = \mu_p(f) + k$.

\begin{theorem}[Non-vanishing]\label{thm:nonvanish}
The correction term $\lambda_p(f\cdot\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) - \lambda_p(f) =
c\cdot\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = ck$ is nonzero if and only if $c \neq 0$ and
$\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = k \neq 0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A product $ck$ of nonnegative integers is nonzero iff both factors are; since
$\mu_p(\mathrm{twist}_{c,k}) = k$, this is exactly $c\neq0$ and $\mu\neq0$.
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms}
Given $f = \sum_i a_i X^i$: (i) $\mu_p(f) = v_p(\gcd_i a_i)$; (ii) $\lambda_p(f)$
is the least index $i$ with $v_p(a_i) = \mu_p(f)$, equivalently the trailing
degree of the mod-$p$ reduction of the primitive part $a_i/\gcd_j a_j$. Both run
in $O(d\cdot M)$ for degree $d$ and coefficient cost $M$, and make the additivity
theorems computationally verifiable.

\section{Applications and discussion}
The additivity bridge underlies the reduction of global invariant computations to
local ones via factorization; the twist formula quantifies the $\lambda$-response
to a multiplicative twist and pinpoints its $\mu$-dependence. The proof cleanly
separates the two invariants into two mathematical worlds --- content/valuation
for $\mu$, finite-field trailing degree for $\lambda$. The supersingular theory of
Pollack and Sprung, Matsuno's twist comparison, and non-vanishing $\mu$ phenomena
form the arithmetic backdrop; we isolate and prove their algebraic core.

\section{Future directions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Move from $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ to $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}_p[[T]]$, replacing content
by the $p$-adic valuation of a power series and trailing degree by the
distinguished-polynomial degree from Weierstrass preparation, and reprove
additivity there.
\item Model the sharp/flat pair $(f^{\sharp}, f^{\flat})$ honestly via the
Pollack--Sprung logarithmic matrix and derive the sharp/flat $\lambda$-difference,
recovering the $\mu$-proportional term as a special case.
\item Replace the modelled factor $p^k X^{ck}$ by the genuine twisting operator of
a quadratic character for square-free $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, identifying $c$ with
the predicted arithmetic data.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}
The two Iwasawa invariants $\mu$ and $\lambda$ are additive under multiplication
--- one via Gauss's Lemma and $p$-adic valuations, the other via trailing degrees
in $\mathbb{F}_p[X]$ --- and this bridge yields a Matsuno-type twist formula in
which the $\lambda$-shift under a modelled quadratic twist contains a term
$c\cdot\mu$ proportional to the twist's $\mu$-invariant, non-vanishing exactly when
$\mu\neq0$ and $c\neq0$. A non-vanishing $\mu$ leaves an indelible, predictable
fingerprint on $\lambda$ under quadratic twist.

polynomial, represented as a list of coefficients ``[a0, a1, a2, ...]`` for

The module is self-contained: run ``python demo.py``.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from functools import reduce as _reduce
from typing import List


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Polynomial helpers (dense integer coefficient lists)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def poly_trim(f: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Remove trailing (high-degree) zero coefficients; keep [0] for the zero poly."""
    g = list(f)
    while len(g) > 1 and g[-1] == 0:
        g.pop()
    return g


def poly_mul(f: List[int], g: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Multiply two integer polynomials given as coefficient lists."""
    if not f or not g:
        return [0]
    out = [0] * (len(f) + len(g) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(f):
        for j, b in enumerate(g):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return poly_trim(out)


def poly_is_zero(f: List[int]) -> bool:
    return all(c == 0 for c in f)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# p-adic valuation and content / primitive part
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def padic_val_int(p: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Exact power of the prime ``p`` dividing the nonzero integer ``n``."""
    if n == 0:
        raise ValueError("p-adic valuation of 0 is undefined here")
    n = abs(n)
    v = 0
    while n % p == 0:
        n //= p
        v += 1
    return v


def content(f: List[int]) -> int:
    """Content: the (nonnegative) gcd of the coefficients of a nonzero poly."""
    return _reduce(gcd, (abs(c) for c in f), 0)


def primitive_part(f: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Primitive part f / content(f)."""
    c = content(f)
    if c == 0:
        raise ValueError("primitive part of the zero polynomial is undefined")
    return [a // c for a in f]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The two Iwasawa invariants
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def mu_invariant(p: int, f: List[int]) -> int:
    """mu_p(f) = v_p(content(f))."""
    if poly_is_zero(f):
        raise ValueError("mu-invariant of the zero polynomial is undefined")
    return padic_val_int(p, content(f))


def lambda_invariant(p: int, f: List[int]) -> int:

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from functools import reduce as _reduce
from typing import List


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Polynomial helpers (dense integer coefficient lists)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def poly_trim(f: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Remove trailing (high-degree) zero coefficients; keep [0] for the zero poly."""
    g = list(f)
    while len(g) > 1 and g[-1] == 0:
        g.pop()
    return g


def poly_mul(f: List[int], g: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Multiply two integer polynomials given as coefficient lists."""
    if not f or not g:
        return [0]
    out = [0] * (len(f) + len(g) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(f):
        for j, b in enumerate(g):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return poly_trim(out)


def poly_is_zero(f: List[int]) -> bool:
    return all(c == 0 for c in f)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# p-adic valuation and content / primitive part
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def padic_val_int(p: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Exact power of the prime ``p`` dividing the nonzero integer ``n``."""
    if n == 0:
        raise ValueError("p-adic valuation of 0 is undefined here")
    n = abs(n)
    v = 0
    while n % p == 0:
        n //= p
        v += 1
    return v


def content(f: List[int]) -> int:
    """Content: the (nonnegative) gcd of the coefficients of a nonzero poly."""
    return _reduce(gcd, (abs(c) for c in f), 0)


def primitive_part(f: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Primitive part f / content(f)."""
    c = content(f)
    if c == 0:
        raise ValueError("primitive part of the zero polynomial is undefined")
    return [a // c for a in f]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The two Iwasawa invariants
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def mu_invariant(p: int, f: List[int]) -> int:
    """mu_p(f) = v_p(content(f))."""
    if poly_is_zero(f):
        raise ValueError("mu-invariant of the zero polynomial is undefined")
    return padic_val_int(p, content(f))


def lambda_invariant(p: int, f: List[int]) -> int:
    """lambda_p(f) = trailing degree of (primitive part of f) reduced mod p."""
    if poly_is_zero(f):
        raise ValueError("lambda-invariant of the zero polynomial is undefined")
    pp = primitive_part(f)
    for i, a in enumerate(pp):
        if a % p != 0:
            return i
    # Unreachable: a primitive polynomial cannot vanish identically mod p.
    raise RuntimeError("primitive part reduced to 0 mod p (should be impossible)")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The modelled quadratic-twist factor  twist_{c,k} = p^k * X^{c*k}
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def twist_factor(p: int, c: int, k: int) -> List[int]:
    """p^k * X^(c*k) as a coefficient list."""
    deg = c * k
    coeffs = [0] * (deg + 1)
    coeffs[deg] = p ** k
    return coeffs


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def demo_additivity(p: int, f: List[int], g: List[int]) -> None:
    fg = poly_mul(f, g)
    mf, mg, mfg = mu_invariant(p, f), mu_invariant(p, g), mu_invariant(p, fg)
    lf, lg, lfg = lambda_invariant(p, f), lambda_invariant(p, g), lambda_invariant(p, fg)
    print(f"  f = {f},  g = {g}")
    print(f"  mu(f)={mf}, mu(g)={mg}, mu(f*g)={mfg}  ->  mf+mg={mf+mg}  "
          f"[{'OK' if mfg == mf + mg else 'FAIL'}]")
    print(f"  la(f)={lf}, la(g)={lg}, la(f*g)={lfg}  ->  lf+lg={lf+lg}  "
          f"[{'OK' if lfg == lf + lg else 'FAIL'}]")
    assert mfg == mf + mg and lfg == lf + lg


def demo_twist(p: int, f: List[int], c: int, k: int) -> None:
    tw = twist_factor(p, c, k)
    mu_tw = mu_invariant(p, tw)
    la_tw = lambda_invariant(p, tw)
    ftw = poly_mul(f, tw)
    lhs = lambda_invariant(p, ftw)
    rhs = lambda_invariant(p, f) + c * mu_tw
    correction = c * mu_tw
    print(f"  twist_(c={c},k={k}) = p^{k} * X^{c*k}:  mu={mu_tw}, lambda={la_tw} "
          f"(check lambda == c*mu: {la_tw == c * mu_tw})")
    print(f"  lambda(f*twist)={lhs},  lambda(f)+c*mu(twist)={rhs}  "
          f"[{'OK' if lhs == rhs else 'FAIL'}]")
    print(f"  correction term c*mu = {correction}  ->  nonzero: {correction != 0} "
          f"(expected {c != 0 and mu_tw != 0})")
    assert lhs == rhs
    assert (correction != 0) == (c != 0 and mu_tw != 0)


def main() -> None:
    p = 2  # good supersingular prime in the motivating setting

    print("=" * 64)

    # f = 4 + 2X + 6X^2 (content 2), g = 3X + 3X^2 (content 3, trailing deg 1)

    demo_twist(p, f, c=3, k=2)
    demo_twist(p, f, c=1, k=4)
    demo_twist(p, f, c=5, k=1)

    print("\n[3] Non-vanishing summary (correction = c * k)")
    for c in range(0, 4):

                  f"nonzero={corr != 0} (c!=0 and mu!=0 = {c != 0 and k != 0})")
